recall_prompt: Say how you would do this — say what r is, what condition you check, and which formula you use.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find r and check |r| < 1
steps.margin_note: First mark. a = 1, r = 1/3 and the condition |r| < 1 must all appear before the formula is used.
steps.memory_tip: The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so the terms get smaller.
lines: |r| = 1/3 < 1, so the sum to infinity exists

recall.must_convey: That a = 1, r = 1/3, |r| < 1, and the formula S∞ = a/(1 − r) is stated.
accept: first term one and ratio one third
the ratio is less than one so the infinite sum exists
use s infinity equals a by one minus r
ratio one by three, mod r less than one kabatti sum untundi
check the modulus of r before using the formula

steps.why: An infinite G.P. has a sum only when |r| < 1. Stating that condition is part of the method, not an extra remark.
common_mistakes: Using Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) and leaving n in the answer.
Writing r = 3 by dividing the terms the wrong way round.

steps.label: Substitute a = 1 and r = 1/3
steps.margin_note: Second mark. 1 − 1/3 = 2/3, and dividing 1 by 2/3 gives 3/2. Leave the answer as the fraction 3/2.
steps.memory_tip: One divided by two thirds is three halves.

accept: one minus one third is two thirds
one divided by two thirds is three by two
one by two by three ante three by two
the answer is one point five as a fraction three by two

steps.why: Dividing by 2/3 is the same as multiplying by 3/2, which is where the answer comes from. The sum is finite even though the terms never stop.
common_mistakes: Writing the answer as 2/3 by forgetting to invert the denominator.
Taking the first term as 1/3 instead of 1, which gives 1/2.
